quarterly_data.signal: CONTRACTED AI/DATA-CENTER LOAD CROSSES 17 GW. Four large-load projects were signed in the quarter alone: three projects in Alabama where Alabama Power added approximately 3 GW, plus a Georgia Power 3.2 GW, 25-year electric service contract with OpenAI at its newly announced site near Savannah, Georgia. Combined, those four projects represent 6 GW of newly contracted customer load, and together with agreements previously signed they bring total contracted large load agreements across Southern's electric subsidiaries to over 17 GW by the mid-2030s. CEO Christopher Womack framed the vertically integrated, state-regulated model (one-stop shop across generation, transmission and distribution) as the differentiator winning hyperscaler and data-center developer business in the Southeast.
quarterly_data.figure: 6 GW newly contracted in Q2 (Alabama ~3 GW + Georgia Power/OpenAI 3.2 GW); total contracted large load over 17 GW by mid-2030s

quarterly_data.signal: PROSPECTIVE LARGE-LOAD PIPELINE STILL ABOVE 75 GW, WITH 8 GW IN LATE-STAGE NEGOTIATION. Womack: new projects continue to be added to the prospective pipeline of large industrial and data-center projects, 'which remains well above 75 GW.' Beyond the 17 GW already contracted there are an additional 8 GW of projects in late stages, including 3 GW projected to be finalized in the near term; CFO David Poroch said those contracts are likely to go into 2028 and beyond, with a couple of them initiating their ramp-up in 2028 and running into the next decade. Womack also noted momentum migrating west, with 100 MW projects already succeeding in Mississippi and increasing activity there and in Alabama.
quarterly_data.figure: Prospective pipeline well above 75 GW; 8 GW late-stage of which 3 GW near-term; 100 MW projects in Mississippi

quarterly_data.signal: DATA-CENTER LOAD ACTUALLY ON THE SYSTEM IS COMPOUNDING FAST. System-wide data-center load now exceeds 1.2 GW, an increase of more than 500 megawatts over the prior year, and Poroch noted the company 'crossed over the 1,000 MW line this particular quarter.' Data-center usage was 55% higher than Q2 2025 and is up 49% year to date, primarily due to accelerating load ramps from large-load customers. That pulled weather-normal commercial sales up 7.4% in Q2 (+6% year to date) and total weather-normal retail electricity sales up 2.3% in the first half - the highest retail sales growth through June in nearly two decades. Q2 adjusted EPS was $1.13, up $0.21 versus Q2 2025 and $0.13 above the company's own estimate; first-half adjusted EPS was $2.46.
quarterly_data.figure: Data-center load >1.2 GW (+500 MW YoY); data-center usage +55% YoY in Q2, +49% YTD; commercial sales +7.4% Q2; Q2 adjusted EPS $1.13

quarterly_data.signal: GUIDANCE RAISED TO THE TOP OF THE RANGE ON LOAD GROWTH. Management now projects full-year 2026 adjusted earnings to be near or at the top of the $4.50-$4.60 adjusted EPS guidance range, with a Q3 adjusted EPS estimate of $1.50 per share, and reiterated the goal of being toward the top half of the long-term earnings trajectory. Drivers named were increased usage and customer growth, higher AFUDC from ongoing construction projects, higher earnings from equity-method investments, and contributions from Southern Company Gas and PowerSecure, where distributed, backup and bridge power solutions markets for data centers continue to expand.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance $4.50-$4.60, now expected near or at the top; Q3 estimate $1.50

quarterly_data.signal: GENERATION BUILDOUT FOR AI LOAD - 10 GW APPROVED AND GEORGIA ALREADY OVERSUBSCRIBED. Over the past several years Southern has secured regulatory approvals for 10 GW of new company-owned generation resources, including thermal, battery and solar, as well as hundreds of miles of new transmission lines. The first two of several battery sites are in service, and work on three combustion turbines at Plant Yates is advancing toward completion in the coming quarters. Poroch said the company is 'about 1 GW or 2 away from... selling out the capacity that we had approved in Georgia last year', and Womack added that 'the OpenAI contract in Georgia pushes us beyond our recently approved capacity by right around 1 GW' - i.e. the signed AI load has already outrun approved supply.
quarterly_data.figure: 10 GW of new company-owned generation approved (thermal/battery/solar) + hundreds of miles of transmission; Georgia capacity ~1 GW oversubscribed after the OpenAI contract

quarterly_data.signal: OPEN RFPs AT ALABAMA POWER AND GEORGIA POWER ARE INCREMENTAL CAPITAL NOT YET IN THE PLAN. Ongoing RFPs at both utilities are procuring additional generation for the early 2030s. Poroch was explicit that 'there is not placeholders in our capital plan... the RFPs that are open in Alabama, the RFPs that are open in Georgia, none of that is contemplated in our capital forecast at the moment,' and gave a sizing rule of thumb of 'about $2 billion or so, a little bit above maybe related to 1 GW of new generating capacity.' Timeline: selections known by year end 2026, a certification process running through much of 2027 with clarity in the latter part of 2027, spend feathering in around 2028, and the generation coming online in the 2030-2031 timeline. Alabama runs a near-parallel schedule.
quarterly_data.figure: Capital rule of thumb ~$2B per 1 GW of new generating capacity; RFP selections by year-end 2026, certification through 2027, generation online 2030-2031

quarterly_data.signal: HOW THE AI-LOAD CONTRACTS ARE CREDIT-PROTECTED - ABOUT $21 BILLION OF COLLATERAL BEHIND 17 GW. The large-load contracting framework has four pillars: long-term contracts (the OpenAI contract is 25 years), minimum bills covering at least 100% of the incremental cost to serve, default/termination provisions, and default payments tied to collateral. Poroch said forms of collateral include parent guarantees, lines of credit and surety bonds depending on counterparty credit quality, with the aim of a collateral portfolio equivalent to about A- or better. He initially cited '$20.8 billion of collateral... in the aggregate on full ramp' and then clarified that this refers to the entire portfolio: 'the whole portfolio of the 17 GW, we got about $21 billion of collateral.' Minimum bills effectively decouple revenue from actual customer ramp rates, which Womack said often differ from what was predicted at project approval.
quarterly_data.figure: About $21 billion of collateral in aggregate at full ramp across the 17 GW contracted portfolio; minimum bills cover 100% of incremental cost to serve

quarterly_data.signal: FIRST FLEXIBLE-DEMAND DATA CENTER: 1 GW OF DEMAND RESPONSE AT THE OPENAI SITE. The Savannah site features 1 GW of flexible demand response, and Womack confirmed this is the first time Southern has done that for a data center. Poroch said demand-response flexibility 'does enter into all those conversations' and is possible because the three electric jurisdictions are not limited to a tariff and can negotiate bilateral contracts that price hyperscaler flexibility. Womack said technical requirements - how a hyperscaler's operations affect the system and the grid, and whether it can be more than 'just a taker' - are raised very early in every hyperscaler conversation, and that peak shaving from this resource benefits the whole system.
quarterly_data.figure: 1 GW of flexible demand response at the OpenAI Savannah site - Southern's first for a data center

quarterly_data.signal: NEW NUCLEAR: HYPERSCALERS BEING ASKED TO SHARE AP1000 COST-OVERRUN RISK. Womack said the country needs more nuclear units in operation particularly in the mid-2030s, credited the administration for regulatory actions and for convening groups around long-lead-time items, but stated plainly that 'Southern Company is not going to be next' on a new nuclear build. Asked whether hyperscalers are willing to absorb cost overruns above budgeted amounts for AP1000s, he said he did not want to get ahead of a firm conclusion but 'yes, we are having conversations with them in terms of what role they can play.'

SOUTHERN POWER TOLLING AGREEMENTS ROLLING OFF ARE BEING RE-AIMED AT HYPERSCALERS. As existing tolling agreements expire, Womack said the team is in the midst of recontracting conversations with a host of counterparties, screened for creditworthiness, and sees upside in pricing versus where the contracts were originally struck - contributing to the durability and length of the long-term plan. Poroch added that conversations with both current and new Southern Power counterparties are 'proving to be very fruitful', covering repricing of expiring contracts into the next decade plus the previously announced uprate/brownfield opportunities, with an update expected later in the year; the business will not 'build something and see who shows up.'

ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT ANNOUNCEMENTS IN THE TERRITORY RAN AT THE SECOND-HIGHEST LEVEL EVER. In the last quarter alone, announcements were made for nearly $14 billion of investment and more than 3,000 new jobs across Southern's electric territories, led by several new data-center facilities in Alabama and a new Amazon warehouse in Georgia - the second-highest investment level ever recorded in the electric territories. Womack said there are no state-level moratoriums on data centers in the territory (though some counties have them) and that hyperscalers need to do a better job explaining the benefits, pointing to the OpenAI announcement as the template for community and rate-stability messaging.
quarterly_data.figure: Nearly $14 billion of announced investment and more than 3,000 new jobs in the quarter, led by new data-center facilities in Alabama

connects_to.relationship: long-term electric service supply to OpenAI's Savannah, Georgia data-center campus (Georgia Power)

contracts.signal: Georgia Power signed a 3.2 GW, 25-year contract for electric service with OpenAI at OpenAI's recently announced site near Savannah, Georgia. The site is expected to take electric service in phases beginning in 2028 and features 1 GW of flexible demand response to support reliability when system demand is highest - Southern's first flexible-demand arrangement with a data center. The contract carries the standard large-load framework: minimum bills covering at least 100% of the incremental cost to serve, termination/default payments backed by collateral (lines of credit and surety bonds in this case) targeting an A- or better equivalent position. Womack noted the contract pushes Georgia beyond its recently approved generation capacity by right around 1 GW.
contracts.units: 3.2 GW of contracted load, including 1 GW of flexible demand response; service phased in beginning 2028
